title: Shah Rukh Khan Just Locked Christmas. He's Bringing His Daughter — and Picking a Fight With Marvel.
excerpt: King arrives December 25, putting SRK's first lead role in three years and Suhana Khan's theatrical debut on a collision course with Avengers, Dune 3, and Jumanji. For the diaspora, the only fight that matters is the one in their own cineplex.
body:
There's a particular kind of hush that falls over an NRI WhatsApp group when Shah Rukh Khan announces a release date. It happened again this week. King is officially locked for December 24, 2026 — a global, IMAX-saturated, family-holiday Christmas release — and the man who has owned that corridor more times than anyone in Hindi cinema is walking back into it after a three-year absence that has felt, to his diaspora faithful, like a small eternity.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=M3mfut2RdHk

This is SRK's first leading role since Dunki in December 2023. Three years. For a star who reinvented his entire second act in 2023 with the Pathaan-Jawan-Dunki trifecta — back-to-back-to-back, a comeback with no modern precedent — the wait has been the whole point. Scarcity is its own kind of glamour, and nobody understands that better than the Badshah.

Reports suggest the film is inspired by Léon: The Professional, with SRK playing a sleek, deadly assassin and Suhana portraying his protégé.

And here is where it stops being just another action thriller. King marks the full-fledged theatrical debut of Suhana Khan — not a glorified cameo, not a soft launch, but a co-lead sharing the frame with her father. The premise borrows the bones of Léon: a weathered, lethal assassin takes a young woman under his wing after tragedy upends her life. Casting your own daughter as the apprentice to your killer is the kind of meta-flourish that practically writes its own opening-weekend think-pieces. The internet has already decided this is either the most beautiful father-daughter passing-of-the-torch in Bollywood history or a nepotism lightning rod. Probably both. That tension is exactly why people will buy tickets.

Director Siddharth Anand — who turned SRK into a slick, globe-trotting action god with Pathaan — is back behind the camera, which tells you the visual grammar here: virgin European locations, premium-format scale, and SRK shot like the matinee idol he has refused to stop being at 60. The ensemble reads like a Red Chillies dinner party that got out of hand: Deepika Padukone as the female lead (and the Pathaan chemistry that broke the internet is fully back in play), Abhishek Bachchan as the antagonist, plus Anil Kapoor, Jackie Shroff, Arshad Warsi, Jaideep Ahlawat, Raghav Juyal, and Abhay Verma circling the edges. Anirudh Ravichander, fresh off Jawan, scores. The budget is reportedly ₹350 crore. Nobody is being subtle.

The date itself is a chess move. The makers reportedly skipped an early-December window to leave a deliberate *45-day gap from Nitesh Tiwari's Ramayana*, Diwali's divine epic — a quiet acknowledgment that two tentpoles this size shouldn't bleed each other. But by claiming the Christmas-Eve window, King* walks straight into a Hollywood ambush. Avengers: Doomsday* and Dune 3 land December 18; Dwayne Johnson's Jumanji: Open World opens December 25, the exact same day. For the first time in a long time, SRK isn't the biggest thing in the multiplex lobby. He's in a knife fight for IMAX and premium-large-format screens — the very real estate that fuels his record-shattering overseas numbers.

Because that's the part that hits home for readers in New Jersey, Toronto, and Wembley. Shah Rukh Khan isn't just a Bollywood star to the diaspora — he is the shared cultural password, the actor whose films turned a homesick Friday night into an event at the local Cinemark. The Middle East, North America, and the UK are his fortresses, built on theatrical saturation and near-monopoly control of the best screens. This Christmas, that monopoly is under siege. The question isn't whether NRIs will show up for King — they will, in saris and Santa hats, opening-night first-day-first-show. The question is whether their neighborhood theatre will give SRK the IMAX slot or hand it to Thanos.

The smart money says SRK finds a way. He always does. But for once, the most magnetic man in Indian cinema has to earn the throne the title promises. Christmas Eve, somewhere between the gift wrap and the biryani, the diaspora will find out if the King still rules the room.
